abstract: The correctness of type-checking implementations for proof assistants based on dependent type theory relies on metatheoretical properties that ensure the decidability of typing, some of which require substantial logical strength. Recent mechanizations of such algorithms have highlighted the importance of separating the algorithmic components of the proof - often intricate but requiring relatively low logical strength - from the logical components, which depend on stronger metatheoretical properties, such as normalization or the injectivity of type constructors. In this work, we revisit the logical relations technique and show how it can be used to derive these metatheoretical properties in a direct and uniform way for a core dependent type theory featuring Π-types, N, ⊥ and a universe U. Our presentation yields a compact and conceptually simplified argument that isolates the logically strong reasoning from the algorithmic core. We argue that this approach scales smoothly to richer type theories, and demonstrate this by extending our construction to Exceptional Type Theory (ExcTT), obtaining the first mechanized canonicity proof for this theory.

      Abstract
The correctness of type-checking implementations for proof assistants based on dependent type
theory relies on metatheoretical properties that ensure the decidability of typing, some of which
require substantial logical strength. Recent mechanizations of such algorithms have highlighted the
importance of separating the algorithmic components of the proof – often intricate but requiring
relatively low logical strength – from the logical components, which depend on stronger metathe-
oretical properties, such as normalization or the injectivity of type constructors. In this work, we
revisit the logical relations technique and show how it can be used to derive these metatheoretical
properties in a direct and uniform way for a core dependent type theory featuring Π-types, N, ⊥
and a universe U. Our presentation yields a compact and conceptually simplified argument that
isolates the logically strong reasoning from the algorithmic core. We argue that this approach scales
smoothly to richer type theories, and demonstrate this by extending our construction to Exceptional
Type Theory (ExcTT), obtaining the first mechanized canonicity proof for this theory.

 1      Introduction
One of the central advantages of proof assistants based on intensional dependent type theory
– such as Agda, Lean, or the Rocq Prover – is the existence of decidable type-checking
algorithms that mechanically certify the correctness of proofs. Ensuring the correctness and
completeness of these algorithms, however, relies on subtle invariants that can easily be
invalidated by seemingly benign optimizations or extensions of the theory.
    This fragility has motivated substantial efforts toward certifying type checkers themselves,
most notably in the Rocq ecosystem [44, 45] and in the on-going Lean4Lean [12] or Agda-
core [33] initiatives. These projects focus primarily on the algorithmic core of type checking,
while assuming strong metatheoretical properties – such as normalization – that lie outside
the scope of the certified implementation.
    Logical relations and related realizability techniques play a foundational role in establishing
these metatheoretical properties. Originating in Tait’s computability argument for the simply
typed lambda calculus [50], and extended through Girard’s reducibility candidates for
System F [21] and early work on Martin-Löf Type Theory (MLTT) [35], logical relations have
been the primary tool for proving normalization and canonicity of dependent type theories.

           More recently, the proliferation of new dependent type theories has renewed interest in
       these techniques, both theoretically and practically. Several large formalization efforts have
       mechanized logical relations arguments in proof assistants, including LogRelMLTT in
       Agda [3], LogRelCoq in Rocq [4], and McTT [26]. These developments typically rely on
       multiple layers of logical relation constructions: either by parametrizing a single construction
       over increasingly precise data, or by composing distinct relations to establish different aspects
       of correctness. As a result, logical relations are used not only to justify strong metatheoretical
       properties, but also to establish fine-grained, algorithmically meaningful invariants.
          In parallel, high-level categorical and topos-theoretic frameworks have been proposed to
       generalize logical relations arguments, including categorical Normalisation by Evaluation
       (NbE) [5, 19, 15], synthetic Tait computability [48], and internal sconing [9]. While concep-
       tually powerful, these approaches remain challenging to reconcile with concrete mechanized
       developments, leaving a gap between abstract proofs and implementable techniques.
           From an engineering perspective, the complexity of logical relations strongly suggests that
       they should be deployed only where they are strictly necessary. Yet identifying the minimal
       metatheoretical assumptions required for decidable type checking is itself nontrivial: many
       properties are intertwined, and their precise dependencies are not always clear. Recent work
       by Lennon-Bertrand [31] pushes in this direction by identifying three key properties sufficient
       to establish decidability of conversion in dependent type theory: injectivity of normal forms,
       deep normalization, and a characterization of neutral conversion. This line has been partially
       pursued by Liu et al. [34], who work in an untyped setting and avoid the complexity of
       full-fledged logical relations by assuming injectivity of Π-types rather than deriving it.
          Such assumptions are non-standard however, and create an unverified gap between the
       usual definitions of type theory and the meta theoretical results. In this work, we explain
       how we pursued those insights to provide a mechanized argument for these core properties,
       by building a typed logical relations argument that precisely characterizes neutral terms in
       addition to its usual properties. This approach clarifies existing formalized proofs by focusing
       precisely on what is needed to prove decidability of conversion, showcasing how we can tailor
       the logical relation to both simple and informative.


       Plan of the Paper

       In Section 2, we present the considered type theory together with a formal definition of the
       three key metatheoretical properties advocated for in [31]. In Section 3, we introduce the
       core of the formalization: a mechanized logical relation establishing normalization in a single
       pass for a core Martin-Löf style type theory with a universe, Π-types, natural numbers N,
       and the empty type. We extend the theory with exceptions in Section 4, showing that the
       logical relation scales to this setting and yielding the first mechanized canonicity proof for
       exceptional type theory. In Section 5, we position our construction within the landscape of
       closely related techniques, both pen-and-paper and mechanized, clarifying the connections in
       the literature. In Section 6, we conclude on future work.


       Formalization

       Our results have been mechanized in the Rocq Prover (version 9.0). Definitions and theorems
       are referred to in the text using the Rocq icon which marks a clickable link that points to
       an online version of the formalization.

In the formalization, the syntax of the type theory is represented using preterms together

       Reduction
       Efficient implementations of type checkers and conversion checkers typically rely on additional
       structure in the underlying type theory to obtain fine-grained representations of conversion
       equivalence classes, most often by enabling the computation of normal forms. Following [31],
       we use an untyped reduction relation ⇝ on types and terms described in Figure 1. Reduction
       is made deterministic by choosing a call-by-name evaluation strategy (leftmost-innermost).
       An irreducible term for ⇝ is called a weak-head normal form (whnf), and can either present
       an introduction form as its head (Π, N, ⊥, U, λ, 0, S) or be a neutral term (whne), which can
       be characterized as a stack of elimination forms stuck on a variable. Additionally, we define
       a partial function whnf that computes the whnf of a term using Rocq-Equations [46] ( ).

       2.2    Metatheoretical Properties
       Lennon-Bertrand argues in [31] that in order to completely certify a reduction-based conver-
       sion checker, the three following properties characterizing normal forms and conversion are
       enough. These properties are not immediately derivable from the presentation of the type
       theory and the main goal of this paper is to establish these results using a logical relation
       argument depicted in Sections 3 and 4.
           The first property provides the main characterization of type conversion.

▶ Property 4 (Injectivity and no-confusion of type formers ). Assume two convertible well-
formed types Γ ⊢ A ≡ B are in whnf. Then, either they share the same type constructor and
their respective subterms are also convertible, or they are convertible neutrals at the universe.

    Property 4 implies in particular injectivity of Π types, a key lemma for establishing subject
reduction that propagates typing assumptions across reduction. The property also implies
that two types with distinct head normal forms will never be convertible, an important point
for establishing completeness of conversion checkers.
    The second property aims to characterize conversion between neutral terms. To state
the property, we must first introduce a distinction between types equipped with an η-law,
an extensionality rule, that we will call negative, and types without such an η law, called
positive. Concretely, we consider U, N, ⊥ and neutral types are positive, while Π is negative.1

▶ Property 5 (Inversion of neutral conversions at positive types ). Assume two well-formed
neutral terms Γ ⊢ a ≡ b : A are convertible at a positive type. Then, they must be the same
eliminations of the same variable with convertible arguments (a full definition is given in
Appendix A.1).

       2.3    Partial Equivalence Relations (PERs) & Dependent PERs
       Since we do not know a priori that well formed types and terms normalize, or even that they
       always have a whnf, we use partial equivalence relations (PERs) to manage this partiality.
       A PER on a type A is a symmetric and transitive binary relation R : A → A → Type. In
       particular, it restricts to an equivalence relation on reflexive points, those x : A such that
       R x x holds.
          The notion of PER also extends to a dependent notion.

       ▶ Definition 7 (Dependent PERs). Let (A, R) be a PER, B : Type a type, and S : {a1 a2 :
       A} → R a1 a2 → B → B → Type a dependent relation. S is a dependent PER when it
       satisfies:
       Irrelevance for all r, r′ : R a1 a2 , S r b1 b2 implies S r′ b1 b2 ,
       Transport for all r : R a1 a2 and r′ : R a1 a3 , S r b1 b2 implies S r′ b1 b2 ,
       Symmetry for all r : R a1 a2 , S r b1 b2 implies S (sym r) b2 b1 ,
       Transitivity for all r : R a1 a2 , r′ : R a2 a3 , S r b1 b2 and S r′ b2 b3 imply S (trans r r′ ) b1 b3 .

          Note how the irrelevance property stems from the fact that we consider our PERs to
       be proof-irrelevant, thus the family of relations is not allowed to extensionally distinguish
       between different witnesses of the base relation.

        3     A One-Pass Logical Relation for Normalization
       In this section, we use a logical relations argument to establish the properties listed in
       Section 2.2. Our logical relation is formulated using PERs, whose inhabitants we call
       reducible conversion witnesses, or simply reducibility witnesses. We write Γ ⊩l A ≡ B for
       the type of witnesses of reducible conversion between types A and B at level l in context
       Γ, and Γ ⊩l a ≡ b : A ≡ B/RAB for the type of witnesses of reducible conversion between
       terms a and b over RAB : Γ ⊩l A ≡ B. As in other formalizations, these relations are defined
       mutually using small induction-recursion [18, 24] (note however that the smallness here is
       guaranteed by bumping the inductive definition one universe higher than expected).
           We first highlight the salient aspects of the logical relation on neutral terms in Section 3.1,
       and then illustrate the construction in the case of function types (Section 3.2). Ultimately,
       we show that this logical relation forms a suitable model of the base type theory, allowing us
       to interpret the syntax into it and derive the desired metatheoretical properties (Section 3.6).
           In practice, we proceed in several steps. We first establish basic properties of the relation,
       including irrelevance, stability under renaming, and the reify-reflect principle (Section 3.3).
       We then prove the core PER properties: symmetry, transport (Section 3.4), and finally
       transitivity. Next, we show that each introduction, elimination, and conversion rule of the

3.1    The Key Case of Neutral Terms
One degree of freedom that arises in most definitions of logical relations concerns the treatment
of reducible conversion for neutral terms. For non-neutral terms, reducible conversion is
largely determined by the requirements of eliminators, which must be able to decompose
non-neutral terms into their constituents. By contrast, neutral terms are simply propagated
unchanged; as a result, no property is strictly required on subterms for the logical relations
argument to go through. The definition of reducible conversion of neutral terms could include
no more information than conversion of these terms. Such a choice, however, would yield no
informative result about neutral terms once the fundamental lemma has been established.
    One major obstacle, compared to the case of normal forms, when defining reducible
conversion for neutral terms is the absence of reducibility information for their subterms.
Indeed, neutral terms may contain subterms at arbitrary types that do not appear in the type
of the neutral term itself, and the induction-recursion principle prevents using the inductive
definition of reducible conversion on those types inside the recursive definition.
    For instance, in the case of a neutral application at the type of natural numbers, one

         5      Comparing Logical Relations for Normalization
        Our logical relation was designed to characterize conversion abstractly and derive only the
        normalization and inversion properties required for further proofs on implementations of
        the type theory. Other design choices, that we discuss now, appear in the literature: on
        the representation of normalization, on algorithmic aspects, proof-relevance and arity of the
        relation.

        5.1     Different Approaches to Normalization
        The statement of normalization usually refers to the existence of normal forms representing
        the equivalence classes induced by conversion. Concretely, [15, 16, 48, 23, 49, 9] obtain a
        normalization function norm that assesses the unique existence of a normal form normA t
        for a term t : A. This normalization function must be sound (t ≡ normA t) and complete
        (t ≡ t′ : A ⇐⇒ normA t = normA t′ ). In mechanized work [3, 4] however, this statement can
        be strengthened with an intensional characterization of the conversion relation between a
        term and its normal form: Property 6 not only requires the existence of a normal form normA t
        but also a witness of conversion between t and normA t using a standard derivation, namely
        one obtained by an alternation of reduction to weak-head normal form and extensionality
        principles. This further characterization is then employed to prove the correctness of different
        implementation strategies for conversion checkers, for instance dropping some of the typing
        information as in Coquand’s algorithm [14, 31], or delaying the propagation of substitutions
        to reduce terms’ traversals.

5.3      Proof-Relevant and Proof-Irrelevant Reducibility Witnesses
Most mechanized logical relations for dependent types, such as LogRelMLTT, McTT or
the present work, enforce and leverage an essential property of type reducibility witnesses:
that they are proof-irrelevant. Proof-irrelevance means that the formalization never depends
on the actual computational content of reducibility proofs, that can then be taken as opaque
black-boxes, as term reducibility only depends on the shape of its type index.
   This is in sharp contrast with the definitions of type reducibility that can be found in
pen-and-paper proofs [48, 15], where instead of prescribing which reducibility witnesses exist
by induction recursion, reducibility witnesses are described by the structure they must be
equipped with – a.k.a. normalization structure. These do not satisfy proof-irrelevance, and
thus the reducibility predicate of typed terms depends on the reducibility proof for the type.
   This has some advantages, primarily avoiding the use of a global reduction relation
external to the definition of the type theory: in our logical relation, reduction is crucial
to ensure that the different reducibility witnesses are non-overlapping, which is key to
proof-irrelevance. Indeed, it is quite remarkable that metatheoretical results can be derived
without referring to any specific operational semantics, although one could argue that in the
proof-relevant case, the proof itself is the operational semantics.

type formers and effects. Another important direction concerns sort polymorphism, as
introduced in the Rocq Prover and studied in recent work [39, 43]. Supporting sort-

bring it closer to the type theory implemented in modern proof assistants. We believe that
the modular separation between algorithmic and logical components advocated in this work
